p.seg: Loss of state and power.
Believing slander without awakening,
ancestral temples were exterminated.
Alas!
Integrity could not be attained,
graves are overgrown with weeds and not repaired,
the departed souls return but have nothing to eat.
Distant, far apart, and disorderly,
the longer the time, the more obscure.
Their spirits are unheard and fly away,
ascend the nine heavens and depart forever.
Alas, alas!

"Rhapsody on the Great Man"
Xiàng Rú was appointed the director of the Xiàowén Garden,
seeing that the emperor liked immortals,
he then presented the "Rhapsody on the Great Man."
Its words say:
There exists a great man,
residing in the central state.
His dwelling encompasses ten thousand miles,
yet it is not enough for him to stay even briefly.
Grieving the narrow constraints of the world,
he lightly takes off and travels far.
Riding on a red banner of white rainbow,
Riding on the clouds, I float upwards.
I erect tall poles from the Gézé marsh,
Massing bright, shining pennants.
Hanging the first ten days of the month as a sash,
Trailing a comet as a tassel.
I wave the guiding bridge to make things incline,
And further wield the *yǐnǐ* to beckon and wave.
I grasp the *chānqiāng* stars as banners,
And unfurl a bent rainbow as a canopy.
Red obscurity blending with dark dimness,
A whirlwind rises, and clouds float.
I drive the *yìnglong* dragon-pulled carriage in sinuous beauty,
With red *chī* and blue *qiú* dragons as outriders, twisting and winding.
They bow and rise, bend and curl their skirts in arrogance,
Crooked and broken, bulging and cramped, leaping and prancing in connected coils.
Luxuriant and mighty, strong and forceful, standing still and mimicking,
Scattered and unrestrained, striding and neighing with shamefaced looks.
They step and pace, creak and pant, assuming postures of twisted beauty,
Cicada-like and coiled, inclining and bending, fearful and trembling, they lean and rely.
Entangled and agitated, shouting and arrogant, treading and stamping the path,
Covered and obscured, leaping and bounding, soaring and rushing wildly.
Rushing and rustling, flourishing and gathering, flaming and blazing, lightning flashing,
Suddenly, the mist clears,
Swiftly, the clouds vanish.
I obliquely depart from *Shàoyáng* and ascend to *Tàiyīn*,
Seeking the Realized Ones.
Intertwining and winding, I turn to the right,
Héng lì fēi quán yǐ zhèng dōng. Rushing waterfalls spread eastward.
Xī zhēng líng yǔ ér xuǎn zhī xī, Having summoned all the spiritual keepers to select them,
bù shǔ zhòng shén yú Yáo Guāng. deploying all the gods at Dubhe (Yáo Guāng).
Shǐ Wǔ Dì xiān dǎo xī, Making the Five Emperors lead the way,
fǎn Dà Yī ér cóng Líng Yáng. returning to Great Oneness and following Líng Yáng.
Zuǒ Xuán Míng ér yòu Qián Léi xī, With Xuán Míng on the left and Qián Léi on the right,
qián Cháng Lí ér hòu Yù Huáng. with Cháng Lí in front and Yù Huáng behind.
Sī zhēng Bó Qiáo ér yì Xiàn Mén xī, I ordered the servants to summon Bó Qiáo and employ Xiàn Mén,
zhào Qí Bó shǐ Shàng Fāng. summoned Qí Bó to command Shàng Fāng.
Zhù Róng jǐng ér bì yù xī, Zhù Róng was alert and cleared the way,
qīng qì fēn ér hòu xíng. purifying the atmosphere before proceeding.
Tún yú chē ér wàn shèng xī, My carriages gathered, tens of thousands of chariots,
cuì yún gài ér shù huá qí. with feathered canopies and erected adorned banners.
Shǐ Jù Máng qí jiāng xíng xī, Making Jù Máng lead the procession,
wú yù wǎng hū Nán Āi. I intend to go to the southern border.
Lì Táng Yáo yú Chóng Shān xī, Passing Táng Yáo at Mount Chóng,
guò Yú Shùn yú Jiǔ Yí. passing Yú Shùn at Jiǔ Yí.
Fēn zhàn zhàn qí chā cuò xī, Confused and deep were their interminglings,
zá tà jiāo gé yǐ fāng chí. a jumble of intertwined axles raced in all directions.
Sāo rǎo chōng cōng qí fēn ná xī, The clamorous, bustling, and chaotic entanglements,
pāng bì yāng yà lì yǐ lín lí. the abundant, swelling, and suppressing sounds connected in profuse disorder.
Cuán luó liè jù cóng yǐ lóng róng xī, Collected, arranged, and gathered, densely clustered,
yǎn màn liú làn tān yǐ lù lí. spreading, overflowing, and seething, exhausted and scattered.
Jìng rù Léi Shì zhī pēng lín yù lǜ xī, Directly entering the Thunder Chamber with its booming, clattering, and deep sounds,
dòng chū Guǐ Gǔ zhī kū lěi wǎi kuí. emerging from Ghost Valley with its cavernous, piled-up, and towering forms.
Biàn lǎn bā hóng ér guān sì hǎi xī, Widely surveying the eight directions and observing the four seas,
qiè dù Jiǔ Jiāng yuè Wǔ Hé. I crossed the Nine Rivers and passed over the Five Rivers.
Managing the blazing fire and floating on the weak waters,
Crossing beyond the floating islets, wading through the flowing sands.
Silently stilling the vast, overflowing waters,
Causing the spirit Nǚwā to play the qín and Féng Yí to dance.
The times seem dim and about to become turbid,
Summoning Píngyì to execute Fēngbó,
And punish Yǔshī.
Looking west towards the towering, indistinct, and desolate Kūnlún,
Directly traversing the Three Dangers (Sān Wēi).
Pushing open the Chānghé gate and entering the imperial palace,
Carrying jade maidens and returning with them.
Ascending Lángfēng and gathering afar,
The proud bird soars and alights in one place.
Hovering low over the Yin Mountains, soaring and meandering,
I finally beheld the Queen Mother of the West (Xī Wángmǔ) today.
Pure white hair, wearing a crown, and dwelling in a cave,
Fortunately, she has a three-legged crow to serve her.
If one must live forever like this without dying,
Even living through ten thousand generations would not be enough to rejoice.
Turning the chariot and returning,
Cutting through the pathless Mount Bùzhōu,
Meeting for a meal in the Dark Capital (Yōudū).
Breathing in the misty air and eating morning dew,
Chewing on the essence of zhī and savoring the beauty of jade.
Solemnly searching and soaring high,
The swirling flood rises swiftly.
Piercing through the inverted reflection of lightning,
Shè fēnglóng zhī pāngbì.
Chěng yóudào ér xiū jiàng xī,
wù yí wù ér yuǎn shì.
Pò qū zhōng zhī ài xiá xī,
shū jié chū hū běi yín.
Yí tún qí yú xuán què xī,
yì xiānqū yú hán mén.
Xià zhēngróng ér wú dì xī,
shàng liǎo kuò ér wú tiān.
Shì xuàn mǐn ér wáng jiàn xī,
tīng chǎng huǎng ér wáng wén.
Chéng xū wáng ér shàng xiá xī,
chāo wú yǒu ér dú cún.

Sīmǎ Xiàngrú
*Měirén Fù*
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú was beautiful and carefree,
and traveled to the court of the King of Liáng.
The King of Liáng was pleased with him.
Zōu Yáng slandered him to the King, saying:
"Xiàngrú is indeed beautiful,
but his attire and appearance
are seductive and disloyal.
He intends to use flattering words to gain favor,
and roams the King's inner palace.
Has the King not noticed this?"
The king asked Xiàng Rú 相如, saying,
"Do you enjoy beautiful women?"
Xiàng Rú 相如 said,
"Your subject does not enjoy beautiful women."
The king said,
"If you do not enjoy beautiful women,
how are you different from Kǒng 孔 and Mò 墨?"
Xiàng Rú 相如 said,
"The ancients avoided beautiful women.
The followers of Kǒng 孔 and Mò 墨, upon hearing that Qí 齊 was offering women, went far away;
upon seeing Cháogē 朝歌, turned their carriages around,
like avoiding fire and water,
and seeking refuge from drowning in the mountain corners.
This is because they had not yet seen what was desirable.
How can this prove that they did not enjoy beautiful women?
As for your subject,
having grown up in the western lands,
and living alone in widowhood,
my house is vast and empty,
with no one to share my joy.
There is a woman to the east of my house,
with cloud-like hair, luxuriant and beautiful,
moth eyebrows and bright teeth,
her face flourishing, her color abundant,
her aura shining, her light rising.
She is always looking west,
wanting to stay with me and share my lodging.
She climbs the wall to look at me,
For three years now,
your servant has been rejected and not permitted to serve.
I secretly admired the great king's noble righteousness,
and ordered my carriage eastward.
On the way, I passed through Zhèng and Wèi,
and the road went through Sāngzhōng.
In the morning, I departed from Qín and Wěi,
and in the evening, I lodged at Shànggōng.
The secluded pavilion of Shànggōng,
was quiet, lonely, and empty.
Its doors were closed in the daytime,
dimly lit, as if a god resided there.
Your servant pushed open its door and entered its hall,
where a fragrant aroma was intense,
and embroidered curtains hung high.
A woman was alone,
elegantly seated on a bed,
her extraordinary beauty unrestrained,
her virtuous nature radiant and glorious.
Seeing me lingering,
she smiled and said:
"What country's noble son are you, honored guest?
From where you come, is it not far?"
Then she prepared fine wine
and presented a zither.
I then touched the strings
and played the tunes of "Yōulán" and "Báixuě."
The woman then sang:
"Alone in my chamber, I feel utterly desolate;
Thinking of my fair one, my heart is filled with sorrow.
O beautiful woman, why are you so late in arriving?
The day is already late, and beauty's colors fade;
How dare I entrust myself to one who is forever selfish?"
A jade hairpin hangs from my crown,
Silken sleeves brush against my robe.
The time is late evening,
Dark Yin is obscure and dim.
The flowing wind is bitter and cold,
White snow flutters and falls.
The secluded room is silent and still,
No human voice is heard.
Thereupon, bedding is arranged,
And precious ornaments and playthings are set out.
Golden censers emit fragrant smoke,
Embroidered curtains hang low,
Padded mattresses are layered,
Horn pillows are placed horizontally.
The woman then loosens her outer garments,
Revealing her inner clothing.
Her fair body is exposed,
With delicate bones and full flesh,
She comes to caress me,
Her softness like ointment.
I then steady my pulse within,
And rectify my heart within my breast,
Vowing faithfully,
"Bǐng zhì bù huí, fān rán gāo jǔ, yǔ bǐ cháng cí."
See *Gu Wényuàn*.

*Cháng Mén Fù*.
During the time of Empress Chén of Emperor Xiào Wǔ, she was favored,
and was quite jealous.
Separated in Cháng Mén Palace,
she was sorrowful and full of grieving thoughts.
She heard that Sīmǎ Xiàngrú of Chéngdū, Shǔ Commandery, was the most skilled writer in the world,
so she offered one hundred *jīn* of gold for Xiàngrú and Wénjūn to buy wine,
hoping for a composition to dispel her sorrow.
Then Xiàngrú wrote a text to enlighten the sovereign,
and Empress Chén regained the emperor's favor.
The text says:
"Ah, what a beautiful woman,
pacing leisurely to amuse herself.
Her soul wanders away and does not return,
her body withers and lives alone.
She says I go in the morning and return in the evening,
enjoying food and drink, forgetting people's hearts.
She is resentful, moving on and not remembering the past,
becoming intimate with those who are successful.
Alas, I am so slow and foolish,
Cherishing a joyful heart of sincerity and honesty.
Wishing for your inquiry and thus advancing myself,
hoping to receive the beautiful sound of your voice, my lord.
Offering empty words and hoping for sincerity,
anticipating the Lígōng 離宮 palace south of the city.
Preparing meager provisions and arranging them myself,
yet you, my lord, would not deign to grace me with your presence.
I live in solitude, deeply immersed in devotion,
while the heavens are vast and a fierce wind blows.
Ascending the Lántái 蘭臺 terrace and gazing into the distance,
my spirit wanders, feeling lost and disoriented.
Floating clouds gather and enclose all around,
the sky is deep and dark, and it is daytime yet gloomy.
Thunder rumbles and resounds,
its sound resembling the sounds of your carriage, my lord.
A swirling wind rises from the boudoir,
lifting the curtains of the bedchamber.
Cassia trees intertwine and mingle together,
their fragrance is intensely rich and sweet.
Peacocks gather and keep each other company,
black monkeys howl and sing at length.
Kingfishers flap their wings and flock together,
while luan and phoenix birds soar north and south.
My heart sighs, unable to find relief,
evil influences grow strong and attack within.
Descending the Lántái 蘭臺 terrace and strolling around,
I walk leisurely in the deep palace.
The main hall is massive, as if to create heaven,
rising densely and towering high.
Leisurely wandering in the east wing,
I gaze upon the boundless magnificence.
Pushing the jade doors, shaking the metal knockers,
the resounding noise is like the sound of bells.
Carving magnolias to make rafters,
and decorating the beams with ornamented apricots.
Displaying lush, meandering trees,
separating the storied pavilions and Chinese parasol trees that support each other.
Applying precious wood for the brackets,
piling up unevenly to support the beams.
At times, resembling a collection of similar objects,
like accumulated rocks about to fall.
Five colors dazzle and illuminate each other,
sparkling and radiant, creating light.
Finely arranging tiled bricks of intricate stone,
resembling the patterns of hawksbill turtle shells.
Hanging silk gauze curtains,
suspending linked cords of fine silk tassels.
Gently stroking the pillars and lintels in leisure,
surveying the curved terraces in their grandeur.
White cranes cry out with mournful wails,
a solitary female perches on a withered willow.
As dusk falls and sight is lost,
sadly entrusting myself to the empty hall.
Suspending the bright moon to illuminate myself,
I depart into the clear night in the secluded chamber.
I take up the elegant qín to change the melody,
playing out a sorrowful thought that cannot be prolonged.
I press the flowing zhǐ and turn it back,
the sound is subtle and then rises again.
I thread through and examine the musical passages within,
the sentiment is impassioned and self-assertive.
Those around me are saddened and shed tears,
their weeping flowing haphazardly.
They sigh heavily and increase their sobbing,
shuffling their slippers, they rise and pace back and forth.
Raising their long sleeves to shield themselves,
they count the past days of misfortune.
Having no face to show,
I succumb to weary thoughts and go to bed.
I gather fragrant rùo to use as a pillow,
and sit on a mat of quán lán and zhǐ xiāng.
Suddenly I fall asleep and dream,
my spirit as if my lord is by my side.
Startled, I awake and see nothing,
my soul wanders restlessly as if something is lost.
The crows of the many chickens sadden me,
I rise and gaze upon the pure light of the moon.
I observe the rows of stars,
Bì and Mǎo emerge in the east.
I gaze upon the lushness of the central courtyard,
as if the frost of late autumn has descended.
Yè mànmàn qí ruò suì xī,
huái yùyù qí bùkě zài gēng.
Dàn yǎnjiǎn ér dài shǔ xī,
huāng tíngting ér fù míng.
Qiè rén qiè zì bēi xī,
jiū nián suì ér bù gǎnwàng.

"Shàng Shū Jiàn Liè" (Memorial to the Throne Recommending Against Hunting)
Your minister has heard that among things of the same kind, there are those with extraordinary abilities.
Therefore, strength is attributed to Wū Huò,
swiftness is ascribed to Qìng Jì,
and bravery is expected of Bēn Yù.
In your minister's foolish opinion,
if such men truly exist,
so too should such beasts.
Now, Your Majesty enjoys scaling steep inclines
and shooting fierce beasts.
Should you suddenly encounter a beast of uncommon talent,
startling you from an unprepared position,
and encroaching upon the pure dust of your entourage,
The carriage cannot even turn around,
people have no time to display their skills.
Even if there were the skills of Wū Huò and Féng Méng,
their strength could not be used.
Dried trees and rotten stumps all become obstacles.
This is like Hú Yuè arising from under the axle,
and Qiāng Yí touching wheel hubs.
How can it not be dangerous!
Even with complete security and no worries,
this is still not something that the Son of Heaven should be near.
Moreover, to clear the road before traveling,
and gallop only after the middle of the road is cleared,
even then there are occasional accidents with bits and bridles.
How much more so to tread through the Artemisia and reeds,
and race through the mounds and graves,
enjoying the pleasure of encountering beasts ahead,
while inwardly having no thought of preserving oneself from danger.
Would the harm not be difficult to avoid!
To lightly regard the weight of ten thousand chariots as not being secure,
and take pleasure in venturing out on a path with one chance in ten thousand of danger,
Your servant humbly believes Your Majesty should not do this.
For the enlightened see afar before things have sprouted,
and the wise avoid danger before it has taken form.
Disaster is often hidden in the subtle and concealed,
and erupts from what people neglect.
Therefore, a common saying goes:
"A family with thousands in wealth,
does not sit beneath overhanging eaves."
This saying, though small,
can be used to understand great matters.
Your subject wishes that Your Majesty would pay attention and carefully consider it.

*Yù Bā Shǔ Xí* ("Proclamation to the People of Bā and Shǔ"):
Informing the governor of Bā and Shǔ:
The barbarians have been acting independently,
and have not been punished for a long time.
They often encroach upon our borders,
troubling our officers and gentlemen.
After Your Majesty ascended the throne,
you cared for the entire realm,
pacifying and gathering the Central States.
Then, mobilizing armies and sending out troops,
you campaigned against the Xióngnú in the north.
The *chányú* (ruler of the Xióngnú) was terrified,
bound his arms in surrender,
knelt and sued for peace.
Kāngjū and the Western Regions,
with multiple translations, presented tribute,
bowed their heads and came to offer gifts.
Shifting our troops eastward,
the Mǐnyuè killed each other.
You also sent condolences to Pānyú,
The Crown Prince entered the court.
The rulers of the Southern Barbarians (Nán Yí),
and the chiefs of the Western Bo (Xī Bó),
constantly presented tribute offerings,
not daring to be remiss or negligent,
stretching their necks and raising their heels,
eagerly desiring and admiring civilization and righteousness,
wishing to become subjects.
The distances were vast,
and the mountains and rivers deep and obstructive,
preventing them from coming on their own.
Those who did not submit have already been punished,
while those who did good have not yet been rewarded.
Therefore, I sent a Commandant (zhōng láng jiàng) to treat them as guests.
Sending five hundred men each from Ba (Bā) and Shu (Shǔ) to present gifts,
protecting the envoy, but not like that,
there was no military action,
or the calamity of fighting.
Now I hear that you are raising troops and enacting laws,
alarming the young,
and worrying the elders.
Furthermore, the commandery is presumptuously transporting grain,
none of which is Your Majesty's intention.
Those who were supposed to go either flee and escape or become bandits and are killed,
which is also not the conduct of a subject.
The soldiers of the border commanderies,
upon hearing the smoke signals and seeing the signal fires burn,
All grasped their bows and galloped,
carried weapons and ran,
their sweat flowed continuously,
fearing only to fall behind.
They faced the gleaming blades,
braved the flying arrows,
resolved not to turn back,
determined not to hesitate.
Every person held a furious heart,
as if avenging a private feud.
Is it that they enjoyed death and hated life,
that they were not common people,
and that they served a different lord than Bā Shǔ?
They planned deeply and considered afar,
were anxious about the nation's troubles,
and enjoyed fulfilling the duties of a subject.
Therefore, they received fiefs with conferred tallies,
and were granted noble rank by splitting the guī scepter,
their position was that of a marquis,
and they resided in the ranks of the eastern mansions.
In the end, they left behind a prominent reputation for posterity,
and passed down land to their children and grandchildren.
Their conduct was exceedingly loyal and reverent,
and their position was exceedingly peaceful and comfortable.
Their reputation spread to infinity,
and their meritorious achievements were recorded and did not perish.
Therefore, virtuous men and gentlemen
would spill their brains and marrow in the Central Plains,
Dew and moisture nourish the wild grass without refusing.
Now, when an envoy carrying tribute arrives in Nányí,
they immediately kill him themselves as a thief,
or they flee and escape, ultimately being executed,
their bodies die without a name,
and they are posthumously named "Utterly Foolish,"
bringing shame upon their parents,
and becoming a laughingstock to the world.
The difference in people's capacity and understanding is,
isn't it vast!
However, this is not solely the fault of the envoys themselves.
The teachings of fathers and elder brothers are not prioritized,
the guidance of younger brothers and sons is not careful,
they lack integrity and have little sense of shame,
and the customs are not kind and generous.
That they are subjected to punishment and execution,
is it not fitting!
Your Majesty is concerned about the envoys and officials behaving like that,
and grieves for the unfilial and foolish people behaving in this way.
Therefore, you have sent reliable messengers
to inform the common people about the matter of conscripting soldiers,
and to enumerate for them the crimes of disloyalty leading to death,
rebuking the village elders (sānlǎo) and those respectful to elders (xiàodì) for their failure to teach and instruct.
Now is the time for farming,
and we are heavily burdening the common people.
I have already personally seen the nearby counties,
but I fear that those people in remote valleys, streams, mountains, and marshes may not have heard completely.
When the official proclamation arrives,
urgently dispatch it to the counties and districts,
causing them all to understand His Majesty's intention.
Do not neglect this.

"Bào Zhuō Wénjūn Shū" (報卓文君書 - Reply to Zhuō Wénjūn's Letter)
Though the five flavors are sweet,
would you rather have rice and millet first?
Though the five colors are brilliant,
they do not overshadow coarse cloth.
In this green garment,
I shall hold your pot.
The Jǐn River has mandarin ducks,
The Hàn palace has trees.
Reciting your joyful singing,
makes me retrace my former steps,
I ought not allow you to waste your youth on me and feel sad about growing old.
"Dá Shèng Lǎn Wèn Zuò Fù" (荅盛擥問作賦 - Answering Shèng Lǎn's Question about Composing Rhyme-Prose)
Combining silk threads to create patterns,
arranging brocades and embroideries as substance,
one warp, one weft,
one note of Gōng, one note of Shāng,
these are the traces of composing rhyme-prose.
The heart of the *fù* writer,
encompasses the universe,
and surveys all manner of people.
This is something obtained from within,
and cannot be transmitted.
See *Yù Lǎn* (Imperial Readings) volume 587, citing *Xījīng Zájì* (Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital).
*Nán Shǔ Fùlǎo* (Refuting the Elders of Shu)
Since the rise of the Hàn dynasty, seventy-eight years have passed.
Virtue has flourished over six generations.
Martial prowess is abundant and widespread,
and profound grace is extensive.
All living beings are soaked in it,
overflowing beyond the borders.
Thereupon, an envoy was ordered to campaign westward,
following the current and sweeping away (resistance).
Wherever the wind of (Hàn power) reached,
nothing failed to yield.
Consequently, the *Rǎn* and *Máng* tribes gave allegiance.
The *Zuò* were pacified and the *Qióng* preserved.
*Sī Yú* was conquered,
*Jǔ Bāo Pú* was taken,
and the road was connected back to *Huán*.
Turning eastward, preparing to report,
(the envoy) arrived in the capital of Shǔ.
Twenty-seven elders, officials, and learned gentlemen
solemnly came to call.
After the greetings,
Jìn said:
"I have heard that the principle of the Son of Heaven's relationship with the 夷狄 (Yídí, foreign tribes)
is merely to restrain them without severing ties.
Now, dismissing the soldiers from the three commanderies
and opening the road to Yèláng
has been going on for three years.
Yet, the work is not completed,
the soldiers are weary and exhausted,
and the common people are not provided for.
Now, we are further engaging with the Western 夷 (Yí, foreign tribes),
the strength of the people is depleted,
and I fear we cannot finish this undertaking.
This is also a burden on the envoys.
I am secretly worried about this for you all.
Moreover, the association of Qióng, Zuò, and the Western Bó with the Central Kingdom
has been going on for many years,
too many to count.
The benevolent have not come with virtue,
and the strong have not annexed with force.
I suspect it is perhaps not feasible!
Now, to diminish the people of Qí to appease the 夷狄 (Yídí, foreign tribes),
to impair what we rely on to engage in useless endeavors,
I, a rustic and ignorant person,
do not understand what is being done."
The envoy said:
"What are you talking about?
If it were as you say,
then the people of Shǔ would not have changed their customs,
But the Bā people did not change their customs.
I still dislike hearing such talk.
However, this matter is of great importance,
and certainly not something observers can easily see.
My journey is urgent,
so I cannot learn the details.
Please allow me to roughly explain the outline to you, Senior Official:
"Indeed, the world must have extraordinary individuals
before there can be extraordinary events;
with extraordinary events,
then there is extraordinary achievement.
The extraordinary
is certainly different from what ordinary people do.
Thus it is said, 'At the beginning of extraordinary events,
the common people are fearful;
and when it reaches its completion,
the world is at peace.'
In the past, great floods erupted,
overflowing and inundating the land,
and the people were forced to move up and down,
living in rugged and insecure conditions.
Xià Hòushì (夏后氏) was saddened by this
and therefore dammed the flooded plains,
dredged the Jiāng River and cleared the Hé River,
scattering and suppressing the disaster,
and guided the water east into the sea,
and the world was forever at peace.
How diligent he was!
Was it merely for the people?
His heart was burdened with worries,
and he personally bore the toil.
His body was emaciated and his skin calloused, without downy hair;
hair did not grow on his skin.
Therefore, his glorious achievements are manifest without end,
and his renown permeates this place.
"Moreover, when a worthy ruler ascends the throne,
is it merely to be petty and narrow-minded,
bound by written rules and dragged down by common customs,
following the recitation of what has been transmitted,
merely to please the present generation?
He must put forward grand arguments and profound discussions,
establishing a dynasty and bequeathing a legacy,
as a standard for all generations.
Therefore, he strives for all-embracing inclusiveness,
and diligently contemplates matters that equal Heaven and Earth.
Moreover, does not the *Classic of Poetry* say,
'Throughout all the realm,
there is no land that is not the king's;
to the very borders of the land,
there is no one who is not the king's subject.'
Therefore, within the six directions,
and beyond the eight regions,
if the abundant overflowing influence
does not reach all living things,
A virtuous ruler would be ashamed of this.
Now, within the borders,
among the ranks of those who wear hats and belts (civilized people),
all have received blessings,
with nothing lacking or omitted.
But the lands of foreign and different customs,
the regions of distant and isolated groups,
where boats and carts do not travel,
and human footprints are rare,
where governance and education have not reached,
and the civilizing influence is still faint,
within, they violate righteousness and encroach upon the borders,
and without, evil deeds run rampant,
and they arbitrarily kill their superiors.
Rulers and ministers are easily replaced,
the order of rank is lost,
fathers and elder brothers are killed without cause,
and young orphans are made slaves,
bound together, they cry out.
Turning inward to their homelands, they lament,
saying:
'We have heard that the Middle Kingdom has perfect benevolence,
its virtue vast and its grace universal,
that everything is given its proper place,
why are we alone left behind?
Raising our heels, we long for it,
like withered dryness longing for rain.'
Even a churl would weep for this,
How much more so for a sage of the highest order,
how could he stop?
Therefore, he sent armies north to punish the powerful Hú barbarians,
and dispatched envoys south to reprimand the formidable Yuè.
His virtuous influence spread in all directions,
and rulers from two directions (east and west) flocked to him like scales, looking up to him like a current,
wishing to receive titles, numbering in the hundreds of millions.
Therefore, he closed the gate of Mòruò,
patrolled Zāngkē,
carved inscriptions on Mount Líng,
and constructed a bridge at Sūnyuán.
He initiated the path of morality,
established the system of benevolence and righteousness,
intending to broadly bestow grace and widely spread kindness,
to gently nurture from afar and guide for the long term,
so that those far away would not be isolated,
those in obscurity and darkness
might receive the light of brightness,
to lay down armor and weapons here,
and cease conquest there,
making near and far into one body,
bringing prosperity to both within and without,
would that not be peaceful?
To rescue the people from sinking and drowning,
to uphold the supreme virtue of the emperor,
to reverse the decline and decay of a declining age,
to continue the interrupted endeavors of the Zhōu lineage,
these are the urgent duties of the Son of Heaven.
Though the common people are weary,
how can it be stopped?
"Moreover, a true king has never not begun with worry and diligence
and ended in ease and pleasure.
Thus, the mandate's sign
lies in this.
Just as they are about to increase the *tàishān* sacrifices,
add the *liángfù* ceremonies,
let the harmony bells ring,
raise up the songs of praise,
to reach up to the five emperors,
and down to the three kings.
The observers have not yet seen a finger,
the listeners have not yet heard a sound,
yet the scorched phoenix has already soared into the vastness,
while the hunters are still gazing at the marshes and swamps.
How sad!"

*Letter in Reply to Qí Hóu Zēng Tā*
I have heard that the ancient sage kings,
understanding that people cannot bear to part with their loved ones,
therefore established rituals.
Now, people transgress them.
It is for this reason that I wish to be buried naked,
to correct the ways of the world.
Indeed, extravagant burials truly provide no benefit to the dead,
yet common people compete to outdo each other,
wasting money and resources,
burying them to rot underground.
Some even bury today and exhume tomorrow,
how is this really different from exposing a corpse in the wilderness!
Furthermore, death
is the transformation of the end of life,
and the returning of things [to their origin].
The returning gets to arrive,
the transforming gets to change,
These things each return to their true nature.
Returning to true nature is obscure and silent,
without form or sound,
and thus aligns with the Way's essence.
Now, embellishing the exterior to impress the masses,
and elaborate burials that obstruct the true nature,
cause those returning (to the earth) to be unable to arrive,
and those transforming (into something new) to be unable to change.
This is to cause things to each lose their proper place.
Furthermore, I have heard it said that
the spirit (jīngshén)
is what belongs to Heaven;
the physical body (xínghái)
is what belongs to Earth.
The spirit separated from the body,
each returns to its true nature;
therefore, it is called a ghost (guǐ).
The meaning of the word "ghost" (guǐ) is "returning."
The corpse remains alone, a lifeless lump,
how could it possibly have consciousness?
To wrap it in silks and brocades,
and separate it with coffins and outer coffins,
the limbs bound and tied,
the mouth filled with jade and stones,
wishing to transform but unable to do so,
it becomes suppressed and a withered waxen thing.
After a thousand years,
the coffins and outer coffins decay and rot,
Then I can return to the soil,
and go to my true home.
Speaking from this,
what use is there in being a long-term guest?
In the past, when Emperor Yáo was buried,
a hollowed-out log was used as a coffin,
and kudzu vines were used as ties.
Its bottom piercing did not disturb the springs,
and its top did not leak out the stench of decay.
Therefore, the sage kings valued ease in life,
and ease in death and burial.
They did not expend effort on what was useless,
nor did they waste wealth on what was meaningless.
Now, spending wealth on lavish funerals,
with layers upon layers of partitions,
the dead do not know,
and the living do not benefit,
this is called a great delusion.
Alas!
I will not do this.

Dǒng Zhòngshū
"Rhapsody on a Scholar Who Does Not Encounter [Good] Times"
Alas, woe is me!
Ah, so distant and remote!
When the time comes, how slow it is!
When it goes, how swift it is!
To bend my will and follow others,
is not the way for my companions.
To rectify myself and wait for the time,
is to be nearing death.
To drift along with the times,
how can one be awakened?
The sorrow in my heart,
does not anticipate reward.
Anxious and without peace,
only increases disgrace.
To strive hard and butt against the fence,
is to only break my horns in vain.
If I do not leave my household,
perhaps I will be free from coercion.
Zhòng says:
I was not born during the flourishing of the Three Dynasties,
but in the degenerate customs of the Late Three Seasons.
The degenerate customs seek advancement through sophistry and deceit,
while upright gentlemen restrain themselves with integrity.
Although I examine myself thrice daily,
I still harbor doubt about whether to advance or retreat.
Those who flatter are indeed numerous,
pointing at white and calling it black.
Eyes trust in beauty, yet words are obscure,
mouths trust in eloquence, yet words are stammering.
Ghosts and spirits cannot rectify the perversity and disorder of human affairs,
Even sages and worthies cannot enlighten the stubbornness and delusion of fools.
To go out, one cannot go along with them,
To keep one's talents hidden, one is scorned for being unaccepted.
I retreat, cleanse my heart, and plead inwardly,
Yet I truly do not know which path to take.
Observing the pure radiance of ancient times,
Even upright scholars are isolated and have nowhere to return.
Yīn Tāng had Biàn Suí and Wù Guāng,
Zhōu Wǔ had Bó Yí and Shū Qí.
Biàn Suí and Wù Guāng hid their traces in deep pools,
Bó Yí and Shū Qí climbed mountains to gather ferns.
If those sages and worthies were so anxious and hurried,
How much more so when the whole world is in a state of common delusion?
Like Wǔ Yuán and Qū Yuán,
I certainly have nothing left to look back to.
I also cannot be like those few,
To travel far away and end my days in antiquity.
Considering the distance of my peers,
I suspect the wilderness is desolate and difficult to traverse.
Fearing the departure of the noble man,
I am warned to abstain from food for three days.
Alas, the world is in universal discord,
Sadly, there is no one to return with.
Why not return to one's original pursuits,
And not follow the world in its endless cycles?
Although feigning virtue might gain a hundred benefits,
It is still better to correct one's heart and return to a single goodness.
Only moving after difficulties press,
How could it be said that my inherent nature is narrow?
Illustrating accord with others and great possession,
Making clear humility and striving to extend it.
Following obscurity in silent sufficiency,
How could I display brilliance and seek fame?
If our livers and gallbladders can be the same,
Why need we distinguish between hairs and whiskers?

*Strategies in Response to the Recommendation of Worthies and the Good in Yuánguāng Year 1*
Your Majesty issues virtuous sounds,
sends down clear edicts,
seeking the Mandate of Heaven and human nature,
all of which are beyond the reach of this foolish minister.
I, your servant, carefully examine within the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
and observe the affairs already carried out by previous generations,
in order to observe the interaction between Heaven and man,
which is truly awe-inspiring.
When the state is about to suffer the ruin of losing the Way,
Heaven first sends forth disasters to reprimand and warn it;
if it does not know to examine itself,
then it sends forth strange anomalies to alarm and frighten it;
if it still does not know to change,
then injury and defeat will arrive.
From this, we can see the benevolence and love of Tiān Xīn (天心, the heart of Heaven) in desiring to stop the disorder of human rulers.
Except for an age of great loss of the Way,
Heaven desires to support and completely secure rulers;
the matter lies in exerting oneself with effort.
Exerting oneself in learning,
one's hearing and seeing will be broad, and one's knowledge will become clearer;
exerting oneself in practicing the Way,
one's virtue will daily increase, and one will have great merit.
These are all things that can be made to return and be effective.
The *Shī* (詩, Book of Odes) says, "From morning till night not relaxing,"
The *Shū* (書, Book of Documents) says, "How flourishing, how flourishing!"
These both speak of exerting oneself with effort.
The Dào (道, Way)
is the path by which one proceeds to governance;
Rén (仁, benevolence), Yì (義, righteousness), Lǐ (禮, propriety), and Yuè (樂, music) are all its instruments.
Therefore, after the sage kings have passed away,
their descendants enjoy lasting peace and tranquility for hundreds of years;
all this is due to the merit of propriety, music, and education.
When a king has not yet created music,
he uses the music of the former kings that is appropriate for the age
and deeply educates the people with it.
If the essence of education is not attained,
the Yuǎ (雅, elegant odes) and Sòng (頌, hymns) music cannot be composed.
Therefore, when a king's achievements are complete, he creates music
to celebrate his virtue.
Music
is that by which the customs of the people are transformed
This transforms the customs of the people.
Its power to change the people is easy,
its power to transform people is manifest.
Therefore, music originates in harmony and is rooted in emotion,
it touches the skin,
and is stored in the bones and marrow.
Therefore, even though the royal way was slightly deficient,
the sound of stringed and wind instruments did not decline.
Now, the Yú Shì (虞氏) have not been in power for a long time,
yet the remaining customs of their music and hymns still exist.
This is why Kǒngzǐ (孔子) heard the *Sháo* (《韶》) while in Qí (齊).
Now, no ruler does not desire security and survival and abhor danger and ruin,
yet there are many whose governments are in chaos and countries in danger,
because those they appoint are not the right people,
and the paths they follow are not the right way.
Therefore, the government declines and is destroyed day by day.
Now, the way of Zhōu (周) declined under Yōu (幽) and Lì (厲),
but it was not that the way was lost,
it was that Yōu (幽) and Lì (厲) did not follow it.
When it came to Xuān Wáng (宣王),
he thought of the virtue of the former kings,
revived what was stagnant, and repaired what was broken,
illuminating the achievements of Wén (文) and Wǔ (武).
The way of Zhōu (周) was brilliantly restored,
the poets praised him and composed (poems),
Heaven assisted him,
and he produced virtuous ministers.
Later generations praised and recited (his deeds),
To this day, it has not ceased.
This is due to diligently and tirelessly practicing goodness.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
"It is the person who can broaden the Way,
not the Way that broadens the person."
Therefore, order and chaos, decline and rise, depend on oneself;
it is not that Heaven sends down a decree that cannot be reversed.
It is because what is grasped and maintained is contradictory and loses its guiding principle.
Your servant has heard that the kings whom Heaven greatly supports and employs
must have things that arrive of themselves, which are not achievable by human effort;
these are the omens of receiving the Mandate.
The people of the world,
united in their hearts, turn to him
as if returning to their parents.
Therefore, auspicious omens from Heaven respond to sincerity and arrive.
The *Shū* 《書》 (Book of Documents) says, "A white fish entered the king's boat,
and a fire reappeared on the king's house,
transforming into a crow,"
these were omens of receiving the Mandate.
Zhōu Gōng 周公 said, "Returning, returning!"
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said, "Virtue is not isolated;
it will surely have neighbors."
These are all the effects of accumulating goodness and piling up virtue.
By the time it came to later generations,
indulgence and dissipation led to decline and weakness;
they were unable to govern and manage the multitude of living beings.
The feudal lords rebelled,
They injure and harm good people in order to contend for land,
abandoning virtuous teachings and relying on punishments.
If punishments are not just,
then evil influences arise.
When evil influences accumulate below,
resentment and hatred are harbored above.
When those above and below are not in harmony,
then the *yīn* and *yáng* are discordant, and monstrous things are born.
This is how disasters and anomalies arise.
Your servant has heard that *mìng* (命), the Mandate,
is the decree of Heaven;
*xìng* (性), nature,
is the quality of birth;
*qíng* (情), feelings,
are the desires of people.
Some are short-lived, some long-lived;
some are benevolent, some base.
They are molded and shaped,
but cannot be made purely beautiful.
There is a source for order and chaos,
therefore they are not uniform.
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said:
"The virtue of the *jūnzǐ* (君子) is like wind,
the virtue of the *xiǎorén* (小人) is like grass;
when the wind blows upon the grass, it will surely bend."
Therefore, when Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜) practiced virtue,
the people were benevolent and long-lived;
Jié Zhòu (桀紂), behaving tyrannically,
caused the people to be mean and short-lived.
That the superiors transform the inferiors,
and the inferiors follow the superiors,
is like clay on the potter's wheel,
subject only to what the potter makes it;
it is like metal in the crucible,
subject only to what the smelter casts it into.
"Soothe them, and they will come;
move them, and they will harmonize,"
this is what is meant.
Your servant respectfully examines the text of the *Chūn Qiū* (春秋),
seeking the beginning of the Way of the King,
and finds it in correctness (*zhèng* 正).
Correctness is next to kingship,
and kingship is next to spring.
Spring
is what Heaven does.
Correctness
is what the king does.
The meaning is that
the superior follows what Heaven does,
and the inferior uses it to correct what he does;
this is the beginning of the Way of the King.
Therefore, if the king wishes to act,
he should seek its beginning in Heaven.
The greatest of Heaven's ways lies in *yīn* 陰 and *yáng* 陽.
*Yáng* is associated with virtue,
and *yīn* with punishment;
punishment governs killing, while virtue governs life.
Therefore, *yáng* always resides in high summer,
and takes as its task procreation, nurturing, and growth;
